title: API versioning and deprecation
subtitle: What really breaks a client, how to change an API without breaking it, and how to retire an old version on purpose.

c.v: Stripe's API moves money for many businesses. Once a business connects its code, it expects that code to keep working for years. A Stripe engineer compared the API to a power grid or water supply: after you hook it up, it should run without interruption.
In a 2017 post, Stripe gave an example of a change that would break that promise. A bank account had a true/false field called
. Suppose Stripe replaced it with a text field called
would break, "because it depends on a field that no longer exists."

Stripe still needed to make changes like that. By 2017 it had made "almost a hundred backwards-incompatible upgrades" in six years. It also said it had kept compatibility with every version since the company started in 2011.

How do you change an API a hundred times and still not break code written years ago? That is what this lesson is about. Stripe's answer used dated versions and a translation layer. You will see both, plus the cheaper habit that should come first.

The surprising ones are changes in behaviour. Hyrum Wright put it this way: with enough users, "all observable behaviors of your system will be depended on by somebody."

A version is a promise you have to keep running. Add instead of change, version only when you must, and switch an old version off only when your logs show nobody is left.
Google's AIP-180 names three kinds of compatibility. Old code must still compile, still talk to the server, and still get "what most reasonable developers would expect."
The third kind hides most surprises.

Headers only help if someone reads them. So log the version and the client id on every request. Then you can answer: "Who still calls v1, how often, and on which endpoints?" Stripe shows each customer the versions its own integration uses.

q.v: You change the default page size of a list endpoint from 50 to 20. No field changed. Is this a breaking change?

options.v: No, because the schema is the same.
Yes. Clients that relied on the old default now get different results.
Only for clients that send a page size.

why.v: AIP-180 says changing a default value is breaking and must not be done. Clients that send their own value are not affected.

q.v: In Stripe's 2017 design, how does an old client get the old response shape?

options.v: Stripe runs a separate copy of the old code for each version.
The client must parse the newest shape itself.
Stripe builds the newest shape, then applies version change modules backwards until it reaches the client's version.

why.v: The Stripe post describes building the response for the current version, then walking back through each version change module.

options.v: Nothing. Any two dates are fine.

why.v: RFC 9745 says the Sunset date must not be earlier than the Deprecation date. RFC 9745 uses an
timestamp, and RFC 8594 uses an HTTP date.

q.v: Which fact best tells you an old version is safe to switch off?

options.v: The deprecation email went out six months ago.
Your request logs show almost no traffic on it, and you have contacted the clients that remain.
The new version has been live for a year.

why.v: Announcements and age do not prove anyone moved. Measured traffic per client does.
